name: The Principle of Faunal Succession
statement: Fossils follow one another through the rock record in a fixed, recognizable order, so strata can be dated by what they contain.
meaning: The principle of faunal succession holds that fossil organisms succeed one another through the rock record in a definite, recognisable, and reproducible order, so that any interval of geological time can be identified by its characteristic assemblage of fossils. Because life has changed and species appear and go extinct in a fixed, non-repeating sequence, the fossil content of a stratum lets rocks of the same age in different places be correlated and lets strata be placed in relative chronological order. It is the fundamental tool of stratigraphy and the basis of the geologic time scale.
mechanism: The pattern was found empirically before it had an explanation: William Smith and, independently, Cuvier and Brongniart observed that each set of strata carried its own distinctive fossils in a repeatable vertical order. The explanation came later from evolution and extinction: descent with modification means new species arise and, once extinct, do not reappear, producing an irreversible sequence. Working with the principle of superposition, which fixes the local older-below-younger order, faunal succession attaches a reproducible fossil signature to each level, letting geologists correlate that order between distant sites where the beds cannot be physically traced.

examples.text: William Smith used fossil assemblages to correlate formations across England and produced the first geological map of a whole country, of England and Wales, in 1815.
Cuvier and Brongniart ordered the alternating marine and freshwater strata of the Paris Basin by their distinct fossil faunas, demonstrating the same succession in a second, independent region.

Species that were geographically widespread but short-lived, like certain ammonites, trilobites, and graptolites, make ideal guide fossils for pinning down and correlating the age of the rocks that contain them.

variants.name: Index fossils
variants.text: Guide fossils, ideally abundant, distinctive, widespread, and short-lived, used to identify and correlate the strata in which they occur; foraminifera are heavily used this way in petroleum geology.

variants.name: Biostratigraphy
variants.text: The dating and correlation of rocks by their fossil content, which, combined with superposition across many localities, built the geologic column and the relative time scale.

whyItMatters: It underlies the relative dating of sedimentary rocks and the correlation of strata across regions and even continents where exposure is not continuous. It is the foundation of biostratigraphy and of the geologic time scale, worked out from fossils in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, decades to a century before radiometric dating existed. It remains a working tool in economic geology, where microfossils such as foraminifera are used to correlate subsurface strata between wells and identify hydrocarbon-bearing horizons.

working.text: identify an interval of time by the characteristic set of fossils in its rocks, not by any single species alone.
match strata of the same age between far-apart sites by their shared fossil content, even without continuous exposure.
for fine correlation, rely on species that were widespread and short-lived, giving both broad reach and sharp time resolution.

limits: Several complications require care. Reworked fossils, older ones eroded and redeposited into younger sediment, can give a misleadingly old age for a bed. Facies changes mean contemporaneous environments host different organisms, so different assemblages at two sites may reflect different habitats rather than different ages, which is why widespread, environment-tolerant index fossils are prized. Gaps and unconformities leave the local record incomplete, so missing faunal zones must be recognised. And structural disturbance, folding, faulting, and overthrusting can place older rocks above younger, detected by independent physical evidence.
misreadings: It is not a consequence of evolutionary theory but an empirical pattern established by Smith and by Cuvier and Brongniart roughly half a century before Darwin, and before any evolutionary explanation existed; evolution later explained the pattern, it did not produce it. The charge that dating rocks by fossils and fossils by rocks is circular is rejected by geologists: the fossil order was worked out independently by direct observation and fixed by superposition without reference to fossils, its discoverer was not an evolutionist, and the relative sequence is corroborated by independent radiometric and structural evidence.
origin: Recognised empirically by the English surveyor William Smith in the 1790s while working on canals, and independently by Georges Cuvier and Alexandre Brongniart in the Paris Basin around 1808-1811; Smith proposed no mechanism, the pattern later being explained by evolution and extinction.
